rationale: Daemon composition and message/queue/schedule transitions share bootstrap and transaction ownership.
A single loop reduces shutdown and state/event coupling risk.

blockingFeedback.summary: Bootstrap supplies empty lifecycle capability catalogs, executor registrations, and interceptor implementations, so configured handlers cannot boot or execute.
Inbound persistence commits before routing publication and enqueue, so a later failure is retried as a duplicate and can permanently lose the message.
Joined-transaction queue enqueue mutates before exact transaction authority is validated.
Queue lifecycle publication depends on an optional personaName payload and misclassifies authoritative queue types as messages.
Repeated or conflicting queue terminal transitions can emit multiple distinct lifecycle events for one authoritative state change.
message.routed.v1 omits the resolved persona reference required for route provenance.
Post-bootstrap startup failures escape the Result boundary and can leak the lifecycle dispatcher and other started services.
Successful subagent signals are rejected by the bootstrap signal router, so valid deliveries retry and dead-letter instead of reaching later signal handlers or projectors.
Bootstrap accepts lifecycle subagent subscriptions that are not also explicitly assigned to the owning persona, deferring the authority failure to delivery retries.
QueueProcessor trusts caller- or legacy-controlled top-level __lifecycle payload data as persona and item-type authority.
Message queue enqueue and terminal transition events derive different correlation identifiers for the same queue lifecycle.
Failed daemon startup can close resources before already-started scheduler or queue workloads have drained, allowing overlap with restart.
Bootstrap accepts subagent interceptor subscriptions even though the synchronous interceptor engine can execute only native implementations, silently losing configured transforms and signals.
Queue and scheduler shutdown drains wait forever when handler or prompt work never settles, so normal shutdown and failed-start cleanup can hang indefinitely.
The event-id plus handler-id signal handoff key can exceed the runtime-id persistence bound for contract-valid identities.
Lifecycle-enabled queue publication remains optional, so scope-less AgentRunner continuation and background-completion enqueues can bypass enqueue and terminal lifecycle events.
A timed-out scheduler tick can resume after a direct stop/start because processSchedule checks running state but not its originating generation after asynchronous prompt lookup.
Drain exceptions are treated as successful failed-start cleanup, deferred cleanup ignores its boolean result, and normal stop can remain wedged in stopping after a drain rejection.
Enabled-mode message and schedule enqueues can still bypass lifecycle publication when manager-owned scope or persona resolution is absent.
A native lifecycle handler attached to multiple personas is added to the runtime catalog more than once and makes valid daemon bootstrap fail.
IPC shutdown discards the newly fallible stop promise, so a rejected or timed-out drain can become an unhandled rejection and interrupt deferred teardown gating.
